content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper combines outlier-robust training and adversarial training to improve the two types of robustness simultaneously. The authors provides both theoretical studies and numerical experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

[1] This paper is clear in writing, clearly explaining all the intuitions, main results, numerical experiment setups, and essential numerical outputs.

[2] The proposed algorithm demonstrates an advantage over existing algorithms when there is noise in the data.

Weakness:

[1] This paper runs experiments on CIFAR-100 using ResNet-18, but only uses a small CNN to train CIFAR-10. I would recommend to supplement with some experiments using CIFAR-10 and ResNet-18. In many other literature, the 8/255 robust accuracy for CIFAR-10 can achieve around 50% (e.g., https://github.com/locuslab/robust_overfitting), which is much higher than the results in Table 1 (33.46%). The sample size of CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 are the same, so it would not be difficult to make the adaptation. 

[2] Figure 1 illustrates the intuition why adversarial training fails when there are outliers. The left panel is clear. For the right panel, is it possible that the standard training and vanilla adversarial training do not work because of poor initialization / poor neural network architecture? 

Another suggestion: could the authors provide a graphical illustration using Figure 1 right panel to demonstrate how the decision boundary changes during the training?

[3] Not actually a weakness or any modification in the paper, but I'm wondering why outliers affect adversarial training. In theoretical studies, e.g.,

Javanmard, Adel, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi, and Hamed Hassani. "Precise tradeoffs in adversarial training for linear regression." Conference on Learning Theory. PMLR, 2020

Javanmard, Adel, and Mahdi Soltanolkotabi. "Precise statistical analysis of classification accuracies for adversarial training." The Annals of Statistics 50.4 (2022): 2127-2156.

Xing, Yue, Ruizhi Zhang, and Guang Cheng. "Adversarially robust estimate and risk analysis in linear regression." International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. PMLR, 2021.

Adversarial training may have some problems, but in general it is good. These papers assume some simple statistical models and do not consider heavy tail problem. Could the authors of this submission provide some discussions whether those theories may fail if the distribution of the attributes has a heavy tail?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written, clear, and of high quality.

There may be some concern since it is only a combination of outlier-robust training and adversarial training. But given the theories and experiments, the weakness in the novelty is not that crucial.

Reproducibility: the authors provide code for the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general this is a good submission. The authors may consider the improvements mentioned in Weakness part. I would also encourage the authors to highlight their contributions, rather than stating just as a combination of two robust training methods.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Outlier Robust Adversarial Training (ORAT) based on a bi-level optimization formulation of adversarial training with a robust rank-based loss function. Theoretically, it shows that the learning objective of ORAT satisfies the $\mathcal{H}$-consistency in binary classification, which establishes it as a proper surrogate to adversarial 0/1 loss. It also analyzes its generalization ability and provides uniform convergence rates in high probability. It proposes a simple algorithm to optimize ORAT. Experimental results on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of ORAT in handling outliers and adversarial attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think this paper has the following strengths: 

1. It first studies the problem of developing models that are robust with regard to the low-quality training data and the potential adversarial attack at inference time simultaneously. The problem seems important. 

2. It proposes a novel method, outlier robust adversarial training (ORAT), which can handle outliers in adversarial training jointly. The proposed training algorithm has the same time complexity as the original AT. 

3. It shows ORAT loss satisfies $\mathcal{H}$-calibration and $\mathcal{H}$-consistency. It also provides a detailed theoretical analysis on the generalization error of training with ORAT loss. The theoretical results seem significant and sound, although I don't check the correctness of the proofs carefully.

However, I think this paper has the following weaknesses: 

1. To simulate the outliers in the training dataset, it only considers adding the symmetric (uniform) and asymmetric (class-dependent) noises to the labels of the training data. It would be good to consider other kinds of outliers (e.g., training examples with covariate shifts). Also, it is not clear if the proposed method could have good performance under training data poisoning attacks or not. I think it needs to at least have some discussions about different kinds of outliers in the training dataset and verify if the proposed method could still have good performance when the training dataset contains those outliers. 

2. For the robustness evaluation, it is less interesting to evaluate the defenses under weak adversarial attacks like FGSM and $PGD^{20}$. In Table 1, it should include the results under the AutoAttack (AA). It is important to evaluate the defenses under the strongest attack. From the results in Table 1 and Table 2, it seems the proposed method doesn't have significant robustness improvement over the existing baselines on MNIST and CIFAR-10. I think for adversarial robustness evaluation, we only care about the robustness under the strongest attack. The robustness improvement under weak attacks is less important. So it would be good to include AutoAttack evaluation in Table 1 to see how significantly the proposed method can improve the robustness over the existing methods. Besides, it would be good to include TRADES [1] as a baseline. 


[1] Zhang, Hongyang, et al. "Theoretically principled trade-off between robustness and accuracy." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is clear and the details of the proposed method and the experiments are included. The proposed method is novel and the theoretical results seem significant. However, the experimental evaluation is somewhat limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a novel method to train models that are robust with regard to the low-quality training data and the potential adversarial attack at inference time simultaneously. It also provides theoretical analyses to show the effectiveness of the proposed method. I only have some concerns about the robustness evaluation in the experiments. Thus, I recommend weak rejection. If the authors could address my concerns, I am willing to raise my scores.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors study in detail the problem of adversarially robust training under label noise, referred to as outliers in the paper. In particular, the paper proposes to utilize the average of ranked range (AoRR) loss to help mitigate the effect of outliers during training, where the samples corresponding to the top-m and bottom-k losses after sorting are not utilized for final training in gradient updates of the parameters. The paper thus proposes outlier robust adversarial training (ORAT), and presents theoretical analyses with respect to H-calibration and H-consistency, alongside empirical evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with different amounts of symmetric and asymmetric label noise.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1) The area of outlier robust training is indeed pertinent, and the paper motivates the techniques introduced in a clear, consistent manner. Given the recently introduced AoRR loss, it is fairly natural to analyze its extension to training under the setting of adversarial robustness, which this paper does in detail.
2) The theoretical analyses presented with respect to H-calibration and H-consistency for the proposed ORAT loss as an adversarial surrogate loss is indeed interesting, and is an valuable contribution.
3) The paper presents an extensive set of empirical evaluations on standard datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and helps establish relative performance over other standard methods. (please refer to weakness below however)
4) Furthermore, the performance over several settings is seen to be largely stable over different choices of the hyperparameters m and k, as detailed in experiments in the main paper and appendix.
Weaknesses:
1) The paper needs to perform a more clear comparative analysis with unsupervised/semi-supervised robust training schemes such as that by Uesato et al. [1] and Kim et al. [2] wherein robust training is performed with relatively few labeled examples. This would be a compelling method as a baseline, given that the labels can be verified for smaller datasets with high-fidelity.
2) Furthermore, the noise ranges of 20% - 40% label noise appear to be fairly large, and are perhaps less realistic to be utilized in a fully-supervised setting, since unsupervised/semi-supervised methods serve as a far superior baseline in such settings. Thus, it is imperative that the experimental section be updated with such comparisons, given that these are highly relevant as an alternative for tackling the exact problem studied in the paper. 
3) Given the large body of benchmarks on ResNet-18 networks specifically on CIFAR-10 for adversarial robustness, the paper could be significantly strengthened by including evaluations on the same, since it can be better compared to other baseline methods more easily.
4) Most concerning however, is the relative robust accuracies presented in Section 5, wherein even normally trained networks are seen to produce non-zero robustness to strong attacks such as AutoAttack, which is completely unexpected. For example, the standard-trained network is seen to achieve 10% on 8/255 AA evaluations, while other networks are shown to achieve around 20%. This might possibly be due to a consistent bug in evaluation, and raises concern for the validity of the remaining results presented.
5) Furthermore, in several settings in Table-1, the natural/clean test accuracy of models is lower than that of the robust test accuracy under FGSM, PGD and CW attacks, which indicates that the evaluations presented have systematic errors. For example under 40% asymmetric noise, natural accuracy is 35.89% while FGSM, PGD and CW accuracies are 44.0%,5 40.85% and 40.33% respectively for the Small CNN on CIFAR-10 for 2/255. This inconsistency is found for several other settings of the table as well, and might indicate that the robust evaluations were not performed correctly.
6) The above point is even more important considering the relative degree of accuracy gain presented over basic baselines of robust training is relatively small and limited across the different experimental settings presented.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper overall is presented in a clear, lucid manner. The method presented is not extremely novel however, given that the AoRR loss was introduced in a prior work.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the concerning aspects listed in the weaknesses section, the experimental section of the paper needs to be revisited in significant detail, both with respect to comparisons with more relevant baselines and related works, as well as with the indication of incorrect robust evaluations wherein robust accuracy is seen to be higher than that of clean accuracy.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In the context of supervised learning using neural networks, two challenges that have been in focus during the last years are (i) the existence of outliers in the training data and (ii) outliers during test time that are specially crafted to increase the test error. One method for coping with the first problem that has been proposed in the literature is the usage of the average of ranked range (AoRR) loss (Hu et al. 2020), which ignores points with the highest and lowest loss values. One method for dealing with the second problem is the adversarially robust (AT) training of Madry et al., 2018. The present paper is motivated by recent observations that the two problems appear simultaneously in practice and proposes combining the adversarial training (AT) method with AoRR. 

On the theoretical side, for the case of binary classification and under realizability, the resulting learning objective is shown to satisfy the H-consistency property from Awasthi et al. 2021. This implies that the objective makes sense as a surrogate loss of the adversarial 0/1 loss, in the sense that any sequence of hypotheses that converges to the best possible objective in the class also converges to the best adversarial 0/1 loss in the class. In addition, a generalization bound based on Rademacher complexity is derived for the proposed objective.

On the experimental side, the paper employs the proposed method for training NNs on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets, where both random noise and adversarial attacks are used. The method is compared against standard training, adversarial training methods and a method combining label correcting with adversarial training. The paper shows that SGD on the proposed objective seems to converge in practice and furthermore the resulting method consistently results in 1-5% better test error in the datasets used.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strength of the paper is that is proposes a natural objective that provides improved test error under outliers and adversarial attacks in real-world datasets.  The complexity of the algorithm is the same complexity as the one of traditional adversarial training, but the experiments show better tolerance to corruptions.

A disadvantage of the method is that the hyperparameters $k$ and $m$ that are related to the number of outliers are currently tuned by grid search. Since their values affect the final error and the amount of outliers in real-world settings is not known in advance, it would be important to have an algorithm that self-selects these parameters correctly, otherwise the 1-5% error improvement that is claimed could not be always achieved.

Another minor disadvantage is (as the authors point out) that the outliers during training come from a distribution (rather than being adversarial). This does not seem like an important problem to me since even random noise was breaking previous work methods.

See also my comments in the next box for some additional weaknesses.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The motivation of the paper and the prior work seem to be clearly explained. The experimental evaluation is very thorough and clearly outlined. There are though a few points in Section 4.1 that do not seem clear and/or correct to me:

*The notion of “minimizability” mentioned below Definition 2 is undefined and it is not clear if/how it is used in showing the main result of the section.

*Does the first line of Theorem 2  (let $H$ be a symmetric hypothesis set consisting of the family of all measurable functions $\mathcal{H}$ ) mean that $H$ contains $H_{all} $? This seems a bit restrictive (and is contradictory to the line below the theorem statement that $H$ could be the class of linear classifiers). Is it needed or do we actually need only what is mentioned in the last line of the statement (that the optimal classifier belongs in the class H)? I also see this assumption in Lemma 4, which is a restatement of Theorems 23,24 from Awasthi et al. 2021, but the assumption is not there in the Awasthi et al. 2021 (and also Theorem 24 of Awasthi et al. 2021 is about the specific $\rho$-margin loss function).

*Theorem 2 assumes realizability, which also seems restrictive, given that the paper considers the outlier robust setting where distributions may have label noise. 

A few minor comments:
*For Definition 2 the authors could cite the original paper (Steinwart 2007)
*In the paragraph above Definition 2: The notation for the conditional probability $\eta$ should make explicit that $\eta$ depends on the given point $x$.

Novelty: The paper follows a natural approach by combining two of the most natural solutions for outlier robust learning and adversarial learning. The analysis of Section 4 follows Awasthi et al. 2021 but requires some extensive case analysis because of the particular loss function that is considered.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper combines a robust loss with adversarial training. This results in an efficient algorithm with better resilience to the combination of outliers and adversarial attacks. The main weakness is that the hyperparameters relevant to the fraction of outliers need to be adjusted manually and also some issues in section 4. These weaknesses make the paper borderline to me, though I am open to revising my score based on the discussion period.
